title: Heredity
subject: science
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 syllabus: heredity; Mendel's contribution - laws for inheritance of traits; sex determination: brief introduction.

blocks.title: Where did those eyes come from?
blocks.body:
People often say a baby has the mother's eyes and the father's smile. Sometimes a child has a feature that neither parent shows, but a grandparent did.

How are features passed on, and why do some skip a generation? About 160 years ago, a monk named **Gregor Mendel** found the answer by counting pea plants. In this chapter you will learn his rules of **heredity**, how genes control traits, and how the sex of a child is decided.

blocks.title: Reading the language of genes
blocks.body:
Har Gobind Khorana was born in Raipur, a small village in Punjab (now in Pakistan), and studied in Lahore and Liverpool. He worked out how the order of the bases in DNA spells out the order of amino acids in a protein: the **genetic code**.

For this he shared the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in 1968. Later his team made the first **artificial gene**.
blocks.future: Genetics leads to careers in medicine, genetic counselling, plant and animal breeding, forensic science and biotechnology.

blocks.question: Two tall pea plants are crossed and some of their offspring are short. What does this tell you?
options: Both parents carried a hidden factor for shortness
blocks.explanation: Each parent must have carried one copy of the factor for shortness (Tt), which is hidden by the factor for tallness.

blocks.title: Variations add up
blocks.body:
Each generation inherits the basic body design of the previous one, with small **variations**.

- In **asexual** reproduction, variations are few, coming only from small errors in DNA copying. The second generation shows the variations of the first plus its own.
- In **sexual** reproduction, DNA from two parents combines, so there is much more variety.

Not all variations are equally useful. Depending on the environment, some variants have an advantage: for example, bacteria that can stand heat survive a heat wave better. The environment **selects** such variants, and this is the basis of **evolution**.

In an asexually reproducing population, a variation found in more individuals has usually been passed on for more generations, so it probably **arose earlier**.

blocks.question: Which kind of reproduction produces more variation?
blocks.explanation: Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents, while asexual reproduction depends only on small copying errors.
option_feedback: Sexual reproduction mixes DNA from two parents.
Asexual reproduction gives only small copying variations.

blocks.title: Dominant and recessive
blocks.body:
**Gregor Johann Mendel (1822–1884)** grew garden peas and was the first to **count** how many plants showed each trait in each generation. He used contrasting traits: tall/short plants, round/wrinkled seeds, violet/white flowers.

- He crossed a pure **tall** plant with a pure **short** plant. All the first-generation (**F1**) plants were tall; there were no medium-height plants.
- When F1 plants were **self-pollinated**, the second generation (**F2**) had both tall and short plants, in the ratio **3 tall : 1 short**.

So both traits were inherited in F1, but only tallness was **expressed**. Mendel proposed that each trait is controlled by **two copies of a factor** (now called **genes**), one from each parent. A single copy of **T** is enough to make the plant tall (**dominant**); both copies must be **t** for the plant to be short (**recessive**).

The F2 plants are **TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1** (genotype), which look **3 tall : 1 short** (phenotype).

blocks.title: Crossing two F1 plants (Tt × Tt)
blocks.body:
| Gametes | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | TT (tall) | Tt (tall) |
| **t** | Tt (tall) | tt (short) |

blocks.question: In Mendel's cross of pure tall and pure short plants, what fraction of the F2 plants were short?
blocks.explanation: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt: only tt (one in four) is short.
option_feedback: Only tt is short: one box in four.

blocks.title: Independent inheritance
blocks.body:
Mendel then crossed plants differing in **two** traits: a tall plant with round seeds and a short plant with wrinkled seeds. All the F1 plants were tall with round seeds, so tallness and round seeds are dominant.

When the F1 plants were self-pollinated, the F2 had tall-round and short-wrinkled plants, but also **new combinations**: tall-wrinkled and short-round. This shows that the traits are **inherited independently**: the factor for height does not travel with the factor for seed shape.

For seed shape (R round, r wrinkled) and seed colour (Y yellow, y green), an F1 plant RrYy makes four kinds of gametes: RY, Ry, rY and ry. Crossing two such plants gives **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**.

blocks.title: F2 of a cross with two traits (RrYy × RrYy)
blocks.body:
| Gametes | RY | Ry | rY | ry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RY** | RRYY | RRYy | RrYY | RrYy |
| **Ry** | RRYy | RRyy | RrYy | Rryy |
| **rY** | RrYY | RrYy | rrYY | rrYy |
| **ry** | RrYy | Rryy | rrYy | rryy |

blocks.question: Which gametes can a plant with genotype RrYy produce?
blocks.explanation: Each gamete gets one copy of each gene, in every combination: RY, Ry, rY and ry.
option_feedback: A gamete has one copy of each gene.
The genes separate independently, giving Ry and rY too.
A gamete has one copy of each gene, not two of one.

blocks.title: Genes, proteins and traits
blocks.body:
The cell's DNA carries the information for making proteins. A section of DNA that provides the information for one protein is a **gene**.

**Example, plant height:** plants have hormones that trigger growth. The amount of hormone depends on how efficiently an **enzyme** makes it. If the gene for the enzyme works well, plenty of hormone is made and the plant is tall. If the gene has an alteration that makes the enzyme less efficient, less hormone is made and the plant is short. So genes control characteristics (traits).

**Why the two copies come in halves:** genes are carried on **chromosomes**. Each body cell has two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. Each germ cell takes **one chromosome from each pair**, so when two germ cells combine, the offspring has the normal number again. This also explains independent inheritance: each pair separates on its own.

blocks.question: A gene affects plant height by controlling the making of:
options: an enzyme that makes a growth hormone
blocks.explanation: The gene gives the information for an enzyme; the efficiency of the enzyme decides how much growth hormone is made.
option_feedback: The cell wall does not control height.

blocks.title: X and Y
blocks.body:
Different species use different ways to decide the sex of a new individual:
- In some reptiles, the **temperature** at which the fertilised eggs are kept decides whether the young are male or female.
- Some animals, such as **snails**, can **change sex**.
- In **humans**, sex is decided **genetically**.

Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. 22 pairs are the same in men and women. The remaining pair are the **sex chromosomes**: women have a perfect pair, **XX**; men have a mismatched pair, **XY** (Y is shorter).

All of a mother's eggs carry an X. Half of a father's sperms carry X and half carry Y. So the sex of the child depends on the **father's** sperm: an X-sperm gives a girl (XX), a Y-sperm gives a boy (XY). The chance is half and half each time.

| Gametes from mother | X | X |
|---|---|---|
| **X** (from father) | XX (girl) | XX (girl) |
| **Y** (from father) | XY (boy) | XY (boy) |

blocks.question: A child who inherits a Y chromosome from the father will be a:
blocks.explanation: The mother always gives an X; X from the mother plus Y from the father gives XY, a boy.
option_feedback: That happens in some reptiles, not humans.
A girl needs an X from the father.

blocks.title: Ratios to remember
blocks.body:
- **One trait:** F2 = **3 : 1** (look), **1 : 2 : 1** (genes).
- **Two traits:** F2 = **9 : 3 : 3 : 1** (all 16 boxes of the square).
- **Capital wins:** one capital letter is enough to show the dominant trait; you need two small letters to see the recessive one.
- **Y makes the boy, and only the father has Y.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
- Writing that the mother decides the sex of the child: the father's sperm (X or Y) decides it.
- Writing the F2 ratio of a one-trait cross as 1 : 2 : 1 when the question asks what the plants look like: that is 3 : 1.
- Writing the gametes of RrYy as Rr and Yy: a gamete has one copy of each gene (RY, Ry, rY, ry).
- Saying a trait is dominant just because a child has it: the blood group example shows you need more information.

blocks.title: Count it in class
blocks.body: Give each pair of students two bags, each with 10 red and 10 white beads (red = T, white = t). They draw one bead from each bag, note the pair, and put the beads back; after 40 draws, count TT, Tt and tt. The class total comes close to 1 : 2 : 1, which is exactly what Mendel did with peas. Toss a coin for the father's X or Y to show the half-and-half chance of a boy or girl.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend why two tall pea plants can have a short offspring, but two short pea plants can never have a tall offspring.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 7:** germ cells with half the chromosomes make sexual reproduction possible.
- **Class 12 Biology:** principles of inheritance and variation, molecular basis of inheritance, and evolution.
- **Everyday life:** plant breeders use these rules to develop better crops, and doctors use them to explain inherited diseases.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
A tall pea plant with violet flowers is crossed with a short plant with white flowers (ttww). All the offspring have violet flowers, and about half are tall and half short.

(a) What is the genotype of the tall parent? (b) Explain.

**Answer:** (a) TtWW. (b) All flowers are violet, so the tall parent must have given W every time: it is WW (if it were Ww, half the offspring would be white). Half are short, so the tall parent gave t to half of its gametes: it is Tt. Crossing TtWW × ttww gives TtWw (tall violet) and ttWw (short violet) in equal numbers.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Variations accumulate over generations; sexual reproduction gives the most variety, and the environment selects useful variants.
- Mendel found that traits are controlled by pairs of factors (genes), one from each parent; one is dominant and the other recessive.
- One-trait cross: F2 is 3 : 1 in appearance and 1 : 2 : 1 in genes. Two-trait cross: F2 is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, showing independent inheritance.
- Genes make proteins such as enzymes, which control traits like plant height.
- Germ cells take one chromosome of each pair. In humans, women are XX and men XY; the father's sperm decides the sex of the child.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Always draw a checkerboard (Punnett square) for crosses: write the gametes along the top and side.
- Learn both ratios: 3 : 1 and 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, and be able to scale them (for example 144 seeds: 81 : 27 : 27 : 9).
- In sex-determination answers, show the cross XX × XY and conclude that the chance is 50% for each sex.
- Read data questions carefully: one family's children are not enough to decide which trait is dominant.
